name: Zhongu
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Zhongu makes no phonological use of vocalic length or nasalization, nor is tone lexically significant. All monosyllables in isolation are uttered in a high (variably level or slightly falling) pitch. With polysyllabic words, a system of stress accent is at work, much as we find in such Amdo dialects as Xiámàn 轄曼 (<Byams.me>; J. Sun 1986) and Hóngyuán 紅原 (<dMar.thang>; Huang 1995). As an expected effect of stress accent, the unstressed (and low-toned) vowel ə in Zhongu often weakens and becomes elided in casual speech (see §2.1). Stress commonly falls on the last syllable of the stem, for example: χse-ná ‘gold’ [...] Complex verbs containing nominal roots or complement verbs exhibit trochaic stress instead [...] As shown by the minimal pair below, however, stress placement is not always predictable and must sometimes be lexically marked: mé-rə ‘ideophone mimicking moving currents’ / me-rə́ ‘to be red’
new_statements.citation: Sun, Jackson T.-S. 2003. Phonological Profile of Zhongu: A New Tibetan Dialect of Northern Sichuan. Language and Linguistics 4(4): 769–836.
new_statements.locator: §2.4 Suprasegmentals, pp. 777–779 (PDF pp. 9–11); minimal pair and fn. 13 on p. 779
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File is the 68-page Language and Linguistics 4.4:769-836 (2003) offprint (title page reads "LANGUAGE AND LINGUISTICS 4.4:769-836, 2003... Phonological Profile of Zhongu: A New Tibetan Dialect of Northern Sichuan, Jackson T.-S. Sun, Academia Sinica"); native text layer; Wayback copy serves the identical 710838-byte PDF (HTTP 200 today), the original ling.sinica.edu.tw URL still times out. QUOTE: present verbatim at the stated locator. §2.4 Suprasegmentals begins at the foot of p. 777 (PDF p. 9): "Zhongu makes no phonological use of vocalic length or nasalization, nor is tone lexically significant. All monosyllables in isolation are uttered in a high (variably level or slightly falling) pitch…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Zhongu has no lexical tone, length or nasalization; polysyllabic words carry a stress accent that normally falls on the last syllable of the stem (suffixes/clitics such as -no LOC, -tsə-kə INDEF-INST, -kə MIR are unstressed, so stem-final stress is not necessarily word-final). Compound/complex verbs built on a nominal root or a complement verb are instead trochaic (stress on the first element: pá-lɛ ‘marry a wife’, ná-ɲɛ ‘listen’, ndʑó-go ‘want to go’). At least one minimal pair (mé-rə vs me-rə́) shows stress can be lexically contrastive. Unstressed syllables are low-toned and their ə is often elided.
new_statements.exceptions: Trochaic (initial) stress in complex verbs containing nominal roots or complement verbs; stress 'not always predictable and must sometimes be lexically marked' (minimal pair mé-rə vs me-rə́); fn. 13: non-stem-final stress is marked with a grave accent in the paper's transcription.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem within the polysyllabic word (suffixes and clitics unstressed); monosyllables in isolation are simply high-pitched. Based on the speech of one main consultant (Gesangmei, Layi Hamlet, Hongtu Township) plus three others; fieldwork 1998–99.
new_statements.identity_note: Sun 2003 describes the Zhongu variety of Hongtu Township (Layi Hamlet, Hongtu Village) in the Zhongu Valley, Songpan County, from one main consultant plus consultants from Zeshu and Jiaochangba villages; this is the only description Glottolog lists for zhon1235 (child dialects Zhongukhok zhon1240, Throchu thro1234 have no separate sources). The earlier world-scan note mis-cited the journal as LTBA 26(1); the paper is Language and Linguistics 4(4): 769–836.

sources.locator: §2.4 Suprasegmentals, pp. 777–779 (PDF pp. 9–11); minimal pair and fn. 13 on p. 779
sources.note: §2.4 Suprasegmentals (pp. 777–779): no vowel length, nasalization or lexical tone; monosyllables in isolation are high-pitched; polysyllabic words have a stress-accent system like Amdo Xiaman/Hongyuan; stress commonly falls on the last syllable of the stem; complex verbs with nominal roots or complement verbs are trochaic; one minimal pair (mé-rə vs me-rə́) shows stress is sometimes lexical; unstressed low-toned ə elides in casual speech.
